text: Azure PowerShell ships as a module called Az, installed once with Install-Module -Name Az. If a tutorial mentions AzureRM instead, that's the older, retired predecessor Microsoft deprecated in favor of Az, which is cross-platform in a way AzureRM never was. Every cmdlet in this lesson comes from Az.

Lesson 21's az login and az account set have direct equivalents here. Connect-AzAccount opens the same browser sign-in flow. Get-AzSubscription is the PowerShell version of az account list. Set-AzContext, with -Subscription, is the PowerShell version of az account set — it fixes which subscription every cmdlet you run afterward targets.

The PowerShell Fundamentals course's Lesson 3 taught Verb-Noun: every cmdlet is guessable from an approved verb list instead of memorized. Azure's own cmdlets follow that pattern with zero exceptions — Get-AzVM retrieves virtual machines, New-AzResourceGroup creates a resource group, Remove-AzResourceGroup deletes one with -Force. If you can guess that stopping a VM is probably Stop-AzVM before being told, that's the pattern working exactly as designed.

Put the same task side by side: az group create --name rg-ps-demo --location eastus on the CLI, versus New-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-ps-demo -Location eastus in PowerShell. Same Azure Resource Manager call underneath, same result — just the CLI's --parameter value syntax against PowerShell's -Parameter "value" convention with an Az prefix on every noun.

Which one you reach for day to day usually comes down to which shell you're already working in, not which tool is more capable — a Windows-admin-heavy shop tends to lean PowerShell, a cross-platform shop tends to lean the CLI. Next: a browser-based shell that gives you both, with nothing to install.
